data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject when the test is a ritual installation whose failure has been planted before the subject is admitted, and it describes its subject when the test is a registry entry added after the subject already exists. The 3-of-26 record is consistent with the hypothesis that only the shown-to-fail-first mutation in compile.py was a planted failure, while every ordinarily-guarded module's guards were added after the code, making them descriptions of the code rather than constraints on it.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a shown-to-fail-first installation is later found in an ordinarily-guarded module that still loses 4/4 to 6/7 mutations, the ritual marker is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a guard written after the code is independently derived from a specification and still passes all mutations, the description-constraint distinction is not purely temporal.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 1-of-9 mutation in compile.py was not actually shown to fail first but was selected by another criterion, the planted-failure mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A planted failure changes the semantics of the test from verification to selection. When a test fails first and the code is then changed until the test passes, the test acts as a fixed target that the code must satisfy. When the code exists first and the test is written to pass against it, the test acts as a restatement of the code's current behavior. The ritual of shown-to-fail-first installation is the observable marker of the planted-failure mechanism; its absence in the ordinarily-guarded modules explains why their guards do not reject mutations: the guards were never given a failure to reject.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
